job.style: a description of a classroom activity or experiment and what it shows

response.passage: In our science lab today, we explored how mobile phones communicate. We learned that phones use radio waves, which are a form of non-ionising radiation. Unlike X-rays, these waves lack the energy to damage DNA or make objects radioactive. When your phone shows a full signal, it actually reduces its transmission power to save battery, meaning it works less hard than when the signal is weak. We also discussed why eyes feel tired after long screen time. It is not because the screen emits harmful rays that burn the eyes, but because we blink less often, causing the surface of the eye to dry out. Regarding battery safety, modern smartphones have smart chips that stop charging once the battery reaches capacity, so leaving a phone plugged in overnight does not cause it to explode. Finally, we looked at the warmth of a phone. A phone gets hot due to the energy used by the processor or battery during heavy tasks, not because it is leaking dangerous radiation. Understanding these facts helps us distinguish between technological reality and common myths about our devices.
response.summary: This activity explains that mobile phones use safe, non-ionising radio waves and that eye strain is caused by reduced blinking rather than harmful rays. It also clarifies that modern phones manage battery charging safely and that heat is a result of normal processing, not radiation.
